opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me, "full-stack" robotics means not treating the problem as a pipeline of isolated modules that different people optimize separately. You have perception, planning, control, learning, the hardware, and increasingly the data infrastructure, and the interesting failures almost always happen at the boundaries between them.

Early in my PhD I worked mostly on the learning and reasoning side: how a robot can break a long-horizon task into subgoals, how it can learn from demonstrations. I kept running into the same issue. You can have a beautiful algorithm, but if the perception representation doesn't expose the right information, or the controller can't execute what the planner asks for, or the data you collected doesn't cover the situations that matter, the whole system falls apart. So I started caring about the full loop.

In my lab that shows up in a few ways. We think about the data-collection side: how to build interfaces and systems so humans can give demonstrations cheaply and at scale, and how to get useful data from people doing tasks naturally rather than only through expensive teleoperation. We think about the representation and learning side: what abstractions let a robot generalize across objects and environments. And we close the loop on real hardware, because the real world keeps you honest. Things that look solved in simulation often aren't.

The other part is mindset. A full-stack roboticist should be comfortable going down to the details: debugging a camera calibration, tuning a controller, or writing infrastructure code. Then they should come back up and ask the big research question. You don't have to be the world expert in every layer, but you need enough fluency to know where the real bottleneck is. In my experience the bottleneck is often not where the field is putting most of its attention. Finding it, and building the system that addresses it end to end, is what full-stack means to me.

r001.rationale: The response says you need not be a world expert in every layer, but does not clearly state that you need not build everything yourself.

r002.rationale: It explains how perception, planning, control, hardware, and data affect whether the whole system works, and says to identify the real bottleneck.

r003.rationale: It calls for fluency across the system and comfort with details in different layers, while clarifying that expertise in every layer is unnecessary.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. When I say full-stack, I mean that I don't think you can really solve robot learning by working on just one layer of the problem. A lot of people pick a slice: they work on perception, or on planning, or on low-level control, or on the data side, and they treat everything else as a black box they borrow from somewhere else. That's a reasonable way to make progress on a narrow question, but it tends to break down when you actually try to get a robot to do something useful in the real world.

My lab tries to span the whole stack. At the bottom, that's the hardware and the low-level controllers, the stuff that decides how the arm actually moves. In the middle, it's the policy learning: imitation learning, reinforcement learning, how you represent skills so they transfer across tasks. At the top, it's the long-horizon reasoning, the task planning, and increasingly the question of how foundation models and language fit into all of this. And cutting across all of it is data: how you collect it, how you simulate it, how much of it you actually need.

The reason I care about spanning those layers is that the interesting problems almost always live at the boundaries. For example, a planner can look great on paper and then fall apart because the skills it's composing weren't trained to handle the states the planner puts them in. Or you build a beautiful learning algorithm and then discover the bottleneck is really that teleoperation data is expensive and noisy, so the real lever is the data collection interface, not the loss function. If you only own one layer, you can't see those failures, let alone fix them.

There's also a practical side. Robotics is unforgiving. A system that works ninety percent of the time is, from the user's point of view, a system that fails constantly. To get that last chunk of reliability you have to be willing to go down into whatever layer is causing the problem, even if it's not the layer you find most intellectually exciting. So full-stack to me is partly a research philosophy and partly just a commitment to actually making the thing work end to end.

r001.rationale: The response says some researchers treat other layers as black boxes they borrow, but does not clearly state that a full-stack approach does not require building everything yourself.

r002.rationale: It says key problems arise at layer boundaries and explains how planning, learned skills, and data collection can affect whether a robot works reliably in the real world.

r003.rationale: It describes spanning hardware, control, policy learning, planning, and data, and says one must be willing to investigate and fix whichever layer causes problems.

astra-6.text:
To me, taking a full-stack approach means thinking about the whole system that allows a robot to do something useful. There’s the hardware, the sensing, the perception, the planning, and the control—and then there’s the learning process that ties those pieces together. You have to understand how decisions in one part affect everything else.

For example, if a robot fails to pick up an object, that’s not necessarily just a learning problem. Maybe the camera can’t see the object clearly, maybe the gripper isn’t suited to it, or maybe the controller can’t execute the motion precisely enough. A full-stack approach means being willing to look across those boundaries and address the actual bottleneck.

So the goal isn’t simply to make one component perform well in isolation. It’s to get all of those components working together reliably in the real world.

r001.rationale: The response describes considering and coordinating system components, but does not say that a full-stack approach can avoid building everything yourself.

r002.rationale: It says decisions in one part affect everything else and explains that failures may come from different components, communicating attention to what affects the robot’s outcome.

r003.rationale: The response calls for understanding the whole system and its interactions, but does not clearly state that this requires sufficiently deep understanding throughout the system.

sol-6.1.text:
To me, taking a full-stack approach means thinking about the entire system that allows a robot to do something useful. That includes the hardware, the sensors, the data you collect, the learning algorithms, and how you actually deploy and evaluate the robot in the real world.

These pieces are tightly connected. What a robot can learn depends on what it can observe and what its hardware can do. And when something fails, it isn’t always an algorithm problem—it could be a sensing issue, a control issue, or a gap in the training data.

So the idea is to let the task guide the design across those layers, and use real-world experience to improve the whole system. Ultimately, we want a robot that can reliably accomplish a task, and that requires more than getting any one component right.

r001.rationale: The response lists system components and says they must work together, but does not state that a full-stack approach does not require building everything yourself.

r002.rationale: It explains how hardware, sensing, data, algorithms, and deployment affect what the robot can learn and whether it accomplishes the task.

r003.rationale: The response describes thinking across the entire system, but does not communicate that understanding must be sufficiently deep throughout it.
